subject: physics
question_text: Draw the P–V diagrams for the isothermal process, the adiabatic process, the isobaric process and the isochoric process.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Short Answer Question 9 (printed p.129). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: PV = constant and PV^γ = constant are both falling hyperbolas with the adiabatic curve steeper because γ = C_P/C_V is greater than 1; the isobaric process traces a horizontal line and the isochoric process a vertical line on the P–V diagram; the area under any of the four curves is the work done in that process. No figure is authored on this card — a text description of each curve is used instead, per the authoring brief's figure-risk note.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The isothermal curve
lines: increases, P falls, and the curve
steps.margin_note: First mark. A smooth falling curve, PV = constant, drawn as a hyperbola.
steps.why: PV = constant is a hyperbola, and drawing it as a straight or a J-shaped line is the single commonest mistake on this figure.
common_mistakes: Drawing a straight line instead of a curve.
Letting the curve touch or cross an axis — it only approaches each axis.

recall.must_convey: That the isothermal curve is a smooth falling hyperbola obeying P V equals constant, never touching either axis.
reject: P V to the gamma equals constant

steps.memory_tip: PV = constant is a hyperbola: it falls smoothly and never touches either axis.

lines: also a falling hyperbola, but at
any point it shares with an
steps.margin_note: Second mark. A steeper falling curve than the isothermal one, crossing it at one point.
steps.why: The extra power γ is exactly what makes the adiabatic curve fall faster than the isothermal one — that is the one comparison this figure is drawn to show.
common_mistakes: Drawing the adiabatic curve less steep than the isothermal curve — it must always be the steeper of the two.
Drawing the two curves parallel instead of crossing at a shared point.

recall.must_convey: That the adiabatic curve obeys P V to the gamma equals constant and is steeper than the isothermal curve at any shared point, because gamma is greater than one.
accept: P V to the gamma equals constant

steps.memory_tip: Adiabatic is always the STEEPER curve — the exponent γ is greater than 1.

P–V diagram, at the height of the
steps.margin_note: Third mark. A horizontal straight line, at constant P.
steps.why: A constant pressure is a constant height on the vertical axis, so the process traces a horizontal line, not a curve.
common_mistakes: Drawing a sloped line instead of a horizontal one.
Confusing this line with the isochoric line, which is vertical.

recall.must_convey: That the isobaric process is drawn as a horizontal straight line at constant pressure.

steps.memory_tip: Isobaric: P is fixed, so the line runs flat, left to right.

steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. A vertical straight line, at constant V, plus the area-under-curve rule.
steps.why: A constant volume is a constant position on the horizontal axis, so the process traces a vertical line — and the shared rule for all four is that the enclosed area under each curve reads off the work.
common_mistakes: Drawing a sloped line instead of a vertical one.
Forgetting that the isochoric process alone does zero work — its line encloses no area with the V-axis.

recall.must_convey: That the isochoric process is a vertical straight line at constant volume, and the area under any curve is the work done.
accept: area under the curve is work

steps.memory_tip: Isochoric: V is fixed, so the line runs straight up. No area, no work.

insider_note: Examiners check the RELATIVE steepness of the two curves at their crossing point — drawing the adiabatic curve too shallow is the most common way this figure loses a mark even when everything else is correct.
